claims.text: The target eutectic high-entropy alloy has a dual- or multiphase microstructure that may include BCC/A2 and FCC or ordered intermetallic phases.
The constituent phases can be classified as mechanically soft and hard phases.
The FCC or ordered intermetallic phase is more electrochemically noble than the paired BCC phase.
At elevated temperature, the alloy initially forms a thin protective oxide layer along phase boundaries.
Sliding wear removes or damages the protective oxide film.
Oxide-film disruption by wear occurs preferentially at interphase boundaries.
The phases exposed by film removal have different electrochemical or oxidation potentials.
Electrochemically dissimilar exposed phases form local micro-galvanic cells.
Micro-galvanic coupling makes one phase dissolve locally more rapidly near interphase boundaries.
Repeated oxide removal followed by localized dissolution produces coupled wear-corrosion degradation faster than either wear or corrosion alone.
The total degradation rate under simultaneous wear and corrosion is greater than the sum of the isolated wear and corrosion rates.
Combined wear-corrosion produces greater mass loss than isolated wear-only or corrosion-only testing.
Combined wear-corrosion produces deeper localized pits at phase boundaries than isolated testing.
The spatial distribution of corrosion correlates with electrochemical-potential contrasts between adjacent phases.
The proposed mechanism requires an initially protective oxide film, electrochemically heterogeneous phases, and a wear rate sufficient to disrupt the film continuously.
The coupled degradation effect should be minimal at lower temperatures or in chemically more homogeneous alloys.
